video_title: The Economic Foundation We Ignore | Frankly Archives 39 (2023)
gist: Nate Hagens re-releases a July 2023 monologue arguing that oil IS the economy — GDP tracks energy and materials at near-100% correlation, and the ~400 billion 'human worker equivalents' delivered annually by fossil fuels are the real source of modern wealth — so the coming constraint shows up first as a financial crisis over unbacked claims, not as physical oil scarcity. He frames crude's 2018 peak (Rystad/Art Berman), the Jevons paradox, and the maximum power principle to argue that EVs, efficiency, voluntary degrowth, and North-to-South wealth transfers cannot work at system scale. A 2026 intro adds that the Strait of Hormuz conflict is accelerating the thesis, with oil stockpiles and storage making new lows.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens states there is roughly a 99% correlation between energy use and GDP and close to a 100% correlation between materials use and GDP, meaning GDP growth is not decoupled from physical throughput.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: If decoupling is a statistical illusion, forecasts of low-carbon GDP growth and 'green growth' equity narratives are systematically overoptimistic; energy demand becomes the leading indicator for global output.
insights.quote: There is, in fact, a 99% correlation between energy and GDP and around 100% correlation between materials and GDP.

insights.claim: Across nations, oil consumption per capita explains about 96% of the variance in GDP per capita on a logarithmic chart, making oil the single tightest macro variable Hagens has found for national income.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Country-level oil consumption trends can be used as a cross-check on GDP forecasts and EM growth stories, especially where reported output diverges from fuel demand.
insights.quote: the correlation on the bottom between oil consumption per nation and the GDP, uh, per nation is around a point nine six R squared

insights.claim: Hagens argues oil's physical properties — high density, liquid at room temperature, pipeline- and ship-transportable, storable in barrels — make it a non-substitutable input rather than one energy source among many.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Supports long-duration exposure to liquid-fuels infrastructure and midstream assets even under aggressive decarbonization scenarios, since substitution is constrained by physics rather than policy.
insights.quote: It's like superhero juice that we can store in barrels and burn and refine and turn into things when we need them.

insights.claim: One barrel of oil embodies roughly 11 years of Hagens' own physical labor, which after handicapping human muscle as about 2.5x more efficient works out to roughly four to four and a half years of human labor per barrel.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete labor-equivalent price anchor for oil: at any plausible wage, crude is drastically underpriced relative to the work it performs, arguing for structurally higher real energy prices.
insights.quote: the amount of work in a barrel of oil is 11 years of my work

insights.claim: Global consumption of about 100 billion barrels of oil equivalent per year in coal, oil and gas equals roughly 400 to 450 billion human worker equivalents, dwarfing the actual human workforce.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Frames energy depletion as a labor-supply shock orders of magnitude larger than demographics, which is the mechanism to watch for structural inflation in goods and services.

insights.claim: The global economy has been adding roughly 4.7 billion new human worker equivalents of incremental fossil energy every year over the past decade, and Hagens suspects future heterodox economists will find this explains much of Solow's residual — the unexplained productivity term behind modern wealth.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: If total factor productivity is largely energy in disguise, productivity-driven growth models break down exactly when incremental energy stops growing — a regime change for long-horizon return assumptions.

insights.claim: Because fossil fuels supply roughly 400 billion worker equivalents to society, Hagens dismisses the size of government subsidies to oil companies as a rounding error by comparison.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Suggests subsidy-removal campaigns are a negligible lever on fossil demand, so policy-risk discounts applied to fossil producers on that basis may be mispriced.

insights.claim: Kleiber's law — metabolism scaling as mass to the three-quarter power — applies not just to insects, mice and blue whales but to countries, whose energy consumption scales at roughly the three-quarter power of their size.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Provides a physical prior for national energy demand growth that is independent of policy targets, useful for stress-testing official demand forecasts.

insights.claim: Under the maximum power principle Howard Odum called the fourth law of thermodynamics, systems self-organize to maximize work per unit time rather than efficiency, so waste is actively selected for in nature and in economies.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Predicts that efficiency-based investment theses underperform, because saved energy gets redeployed into more throughput rather than lower consumption.

insights.claim: Hagens argues the technical friction of EVs and autonomous vehicles — such as stopping two hours to charge — runs counter to humans' primate drive for immediate neurotransmitter reward, which will cap voluntary adoption regardless of the environmental case.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Behavioral time-preference, not battery cost, may be the binding constraint on EV adoption curves — a reason to watch charging speed rather than sticker price as the real adoption trigger.

insights.claim: As an economy adds nodes, the number of energy-requiring connections between them grows roughly as the square of the nodes divided by two, so economic growth compounds energy demand faster than it compounds size.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Implies globalization and network complexity carry a superlinear energy cost, so energy scarcity should show up first as supply-chain simplification and shortened trade routes.

themes.theme: Peak Oil as a Financial Event

insights.claim: Citing a chart built by Art Berman from Rystad Energy data, Hagens says conventional peak oil already happened in 2018, and subsequent growth in total liquids is natural gas plant liquids, which carry fewer BTUs and go into plastics rather than directly into cars.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Headline 'record oil supply' figures may overstate usable transport fuel; watch the crude-versus-NGL split rather than total liquids when sizing refined-product tightness.
insights.quote: peak oil did happen in two thousand and eighteen, at least so far, but we're still growing the total liquids

insights.claim: Hagens expects oil output to decline by about a quarter over the next thirty years, framing the constraint as running out of high-quality, affordable oil at the scale needed to service the system's financial claims rather than running out of oil.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A slow ~25% supply glide path with rising extraction cost argues for persistent backwardation and higher marginal-cost pricing rather than a single spike-and-crash event.

insights.claim: The consequence of oil decline is financial collapse, not oil collapse, because money can be printed but energy cannot — extra money only extracts existing energy faster, so paper claims eventually exceed what the energy system can deliver.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Positions energy depletion as a credit and currency risk rather than a commodity trade — watch for the point where monetary stimulus stops producing physical output.
insights.quote: So the issue with peak oil isn't, uh, oil collapse, it's financial collapse.

insights.claim: Hagens argues the economy is compelled to grow because money is created with no tether to underlying resources and carries interest, so the system will keep degrading the Earth irrespective of climate policy, technology or efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Frames the debt-based monetary system, not consumer preference or corporate behavior, as the variable to watch for any genuine turn in resource demand.

insights.claim: Since 1990 the world has raised energy efficiency by 36% while total energy consumption rose 63%, a live demonstration of the Jevons paradox that efficiency gains of roughly 1% a year do not reduce consumption.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Efficiency-led decarbonization plans embedded in transition scenarios have a 35-year track record of failing to bend absolute demand — a reason to fade demand-destruction assumptions in long-term oil models.
insights.quote: Since nineteen ninety, we've increased energy efficiency by thirty-six percent, and yet globally, we've increased our consumption by sixty-three percent.

insights.claim: Hagens calls focusing on electric vehicles as a climate response equivalent to a personal trainer doing bicep curls during a cancer diagnosis: EVs are cleaner and use less energy but are not a system-wide answer to either climate or energy depletion.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Cautions against treating EV penetration as a proxy for oil demand destruction, since serial refining means displaced gasoline does not remove the barrel.
insights.quote: a focus on electric vehicles as a response to climate is kind of like having a personal trainer focus on bicep curls, uh, while you have a cancer diagnosis

insights.claim: Hagens says the widely cited $5 trillion in fossil fuel subsidies is bunk: about 90% are externalities, 90% of the remaining tenth are consumer subsidies to poor people in oil-producing countries, and within the final 1% renewables receive more actual subsidies than fossil fuel companies, mostly delivered as tax credits.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Undercuts a core plank of the divestment case; policy risk to fossil producers from subsidy withdrawal is far smaller than headlines imply.
insights.quote: That is bunk. Ninety percent of that are externalities

insights.claim: Hagens — who says he left Wall Street over climate concerns — argues climate outcomes are not the fault of the people at Exxon but of shareholders of Exxon, Google, General Electric and Home Depot who optimize for profits that carry no environmental component.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Relocates transition risk from a handful of energy names to the entire profit-maximizing equity complex, weakening the logic of sector-level divestment screens.
insights.quote: It is not the fault of the people at Exxon what is happening. It is the shareholders of Exxon and Google and General Electric and Home Depot, the shareholders are optimizing profits.

insights.claim: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iraq together control over 50% of global oil exports, which Hagens expects to make the contest between financial claims and physical energy control a major story of the coming decade.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Concentration of export capacity in three geopolitically exposed states is the core supply-risk variable for oil, freight and inflation hedges.
insights.quote: Russia and Saudi Arabia and Iraq, the three of them together control over fifty percent of the global oil exports.

insights.claim: Hagens reads the Russia-Ukraine conflict as a shot across the bow of a biophysical phase shift, with Russia trying to destroy dollar hegemony while the US and NATO try to destroy Russia — making a straight-line extrapolation of the last fifty years of technology and growth unlikely.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Argues for de-dollarization and resource-nationalism scenarios as base cases rather than tail risks when building long-horizon allocations.

insights.claim: The UK, once one of the world's leading oil producers, now produces less than half its peak level with only about 10-15% of its discovered North Sea oil left to produce, while investing and saving less than any other G7 country.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Frames UK energy import dependence plus weak domestic investment as a structural drag on sterling and UK real assets, and explains why climate-aware leaders keep approving new leases.

insights.claim: Hagens argues the ultimate wealth of nations is energy and materials, making Russia and Canada wealthy in the long term and the UK and Japan not, since money-printing countries can only buy energy for as long as sellers accept the paper.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A resource-backed framework for long-term currency and sovereign asset allocation: long resource-rich exporters, cautious on import-dependent, low-savings economies.
insights.quote: ultimately the wealth of nations is energy and materials. From that vantage point, Russia and Canada are very wealthy nations in the long term and the UK and Japan not so much.

insights.claim: In his 2026 re-release introduction Hagens says the Strait of Hormuz situation is accelerating his oil thesis, with existing oil stockpiles and storage continuing to make new lows and no end in sight for the war.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Falling inventories against an open-ended conflict at the world's key oil chokepoint is the near-term catalyst that would convert this structural thesis into a price event.
insights.quote: existing oil stockpiles and storage continue to make new lows with no end in sight for this war

insights.claim: Hagens argues there is currently no overlap between the three goals of climate, equity and growth: optimizing for any one of them makes the other two unattainable, so net zero plus Global North-to-South convergence is lip service rather than a coherent plan.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Predicts recurring policy reversals as governments discover the trilemma, which is a source of regime risk for anything priced off stable climate policy.

insights.claim: Expecting humanity to voluntarily degrow is, from a maximum power standpoint, the equivalent of arguing with a forest fire — Hagens says only an insignificant minority will ever be guided by abstinence, especially while other countries can consume more.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Voluntary demand restraint should be excluded from demand models; only price, physical shortage or financial breakdown will cut consumption.
insights.quote: From a maximum power standpoint, um, this is the same equivalent as arguing with a forest fire.

insights.claim: A large Global North to Global South wealth transfer cannot physically happen because the wealth disappears in the process of transferring it — Hagens' landlord could only realize the value of a $400,000 office by selling it while everyone else is forced to sell too.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Implies paper wealth is contingent on ongoing metabolic throughput, so asset values are far more reflexive to an energy contraction than balance sheets suggest.
insights.quote: in the process of transferring the wealth, the wealth disappears

insights.claim: Hagens increasingly thinks the Great Simplification will hit the Global North first, with the remaining extractable fossil carbon consumed by Indonesia, Pakistan, India and other countries after the North's mismanaged financial musical chairs unwinds.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A contrarian ordering for the energy transition: relative demand growth and pricing power shift to South and Southeast Asia while developed-market claims deflate.

insights.claim: Hagens contends that humans in the global market economy have outsourced decision-making to the market, which now exerts downward causation on individuals and on Global North governments that fear circumventing it, leaving no direct policy lever against the superorganism.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Argues that top-down policy interventions will keep being subordinated to market outcomes, so trade the physical and financial constraints rather than the announced policy path.
insights.quote: The market is now in control of all, uh, Global North, um, governments in the world
